newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Parliament clears Israel Chemicals sale.
newsitem.headline: Parliament clears Israel Chemicals sale.

text.p: Israel's parliamentary finance committee on Tuesday gave the Government Corporations Authority the go-ahead to sell a 20 percent stake in Israel Chemicals Ltd.
But one political party asked for another vote on the issue and a spokeswoman said this would be held on Wednesday. The vote was not expected to affect Tuesday's decision.
"The committee approved the government's request of the sale of 20 percent of Israel Chemicals," a committee spokeswoman said. "But a re-vote was requested and will be held tomorrow."

Haim Oron, a member of the committee, said the re-vote was at the request of the Shas party. Neither Oron nor the committee spokeswoman could say why Shas called for it but they said according to parliamentary rules it would have to be held.
Oron said approval of the sale was assured because the Likud and Labour parties, who together are a majority on the committee, were agreed to vote for it.
Industrialist Shoul Eisenberg, who controls 24.9 percent of Israel Chemicals through Israel Corp, has 30 days to exercise an option to buy the additional shares, the spokeswoman said.
Under the terms that he acquired his Israel Chemicals stake in 1995, Eisenberg has right of first refusal to buy the shares.

If Eisenberg does not take the option, the shares will be sold in a single block to a group of investors or sold in small increments in the stock market. Eisenberg's spokesman was not immediately available to comment.
The government holds 48.5 percent of Israel Chemicals and 26.6 percent are publicly traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
Israel Chemicals manufactures fertilisers and chemicals in Israel's mineral-rich Dead Sea area through its holding companies.
A government privatisation plan unveiled last month listed Israel Chemicals as one of the state-owned companies slated for sale this year.

The Government Corporations Authority said it would seek to sell Israel Chemicals shares first because the ministerial privatisation committee had already approved in principle reducing the state's holding to 28 percent.
